sources.entry: Appendix F: Personal Observations on the Reliability of the Shuttle, Richard Feynman

summary.title: Appendix F: Personal Observations on the Reliability of the Shuttle
summary.one_liner: Feynman's Rogers Commission appendix argues that NASA's Shuttle failure-probability estimates were inflated by management, and that erosion, cracks and other warning signs were wrongly treated as evidence of safety.
keywords: risk estimate disagreement management vs engineers
equivalent full power level turbine blade cracks
history of success as evidence of safety
takeaways: Estimates of Shuttle loss probability ranged from about 1 in 100 to 1 in 100,000, with the low figures coming from management and the high ones from working engineers.
Past flights that succeeded despite erosion or blow-by were wrongly taken as proof of safety; such anomalies are warnings of poorly understood behaviour.
A 'safety factor' is meant to cover unknown loads and flaws, so a crack appearing at expected load means there was no real safety margin.
Top-down engine design, where the whole engine is built before components are understood, makes faults expensive to diagnose and fix compared with bottom-up component testing.
Mathematical models built on empirical curve fitting need careful treatment of their uncertainties rather than being trusted as answers.
summary.summary: Feynman's June 1986 appendix to the Rogers Commission report on the Challenger disaster assesses the reliability of the Shuttle's Solid Rocket Boosters, Space Shuttle Main Engines and avionics. He uses historical flight and failure counts, compares NASA, Marshall, Rocketdyne and independent engineers' probability estimates, and traces how certification rules such as the 2x rule and the equivalent-full-power-level limit on turbine blade cracks loosened over time. The text is a prose critique rather than a technical tutorial, and it closes with a section on avionics that this excerpt cuts off before covering.
